samples.result:
The morning light hit the windowsill at exactly 6:47, and I realized I'd been holding my breath. Not for any reason. Just one of those things the body does when the mind wanders too far from its machinery. I exhaled, watched the dust motes scatter and regather in the golden shaft, these tiny constellations that exist only in the angle between a sun and a room.

I've been thinking about angles lately. The way a conversation turns just slightly and suddenly you're somewhere else entirely, looking back at where you stood wondering how you got here. The angle of my father's jaw in photographs from before I was born, when he was still someone I don't recognize, a young man with hope that hadn't yet been tested for tensile strength. The angle of my cat's ears when she hears something I can't, that precise forty-five degree alertness that says *the world is larger than your senses permit*.

My grandmother kept a jar of buttons on her dresser. Not organized. Not color-coded. Just hundreds of buttons accumulated across decades, from garments that had long since dissolved into rags, then memory, then nothing. I would run my fingers through them as a child, this cascading chatter of plastic and shell and metal, and feel something I couldn't name. It was the sound of time being patient. The sound of things waiting for purposes they might never regain. I have my own jar now, though I don't sew. I add to it slowly. A button from a coat I loved that tore beyond repair. One I found in a parking lot, still threaded with a fragment of blue fabric, someone's loss that became my curation. I shake it sometimes and listen, and I'm eight again, and she's alive, and the buttons are still talking.

There's a theory I read somewhere that every cell in your body replaces itself over seven years, which means I'm now composed of materials that never touched her kitchen table, never smelled her lilac soap, never knew the particular creak of her third stair. But the buttons remain. The buttons outlast. I hold one between my fingers and think: *this was fastened against wind, against cold, against exposure*. The original function persists in the form. We are all, maybe, original functions persisting in altered forms.

I walked through the old neighborhood last October. The elm on Crescent Street had been removed, the one we carved nothing into because we were superstitious about permanence, because we wanted to believe we could return unchanged. The stump was still there, wider than my outstretched arms could measure, rings upon rings upon rings. I counted back to one that must have been 1987, the year I was born, the year the tree was already substantial, already doing its slow work of upward and outward while I was just beginning my own. We grew together without knowing each other. We shared groundwater, air, the particular slant of afternoon light in that latitude. Now I continue, and it doesn't, except in the way that cut trees continue in the houses they become, the paper they become, the carbon they release back to the cycle we pretend we're outside of.

I sat on the curb for a while. A man walked past with a dog that looked like it had been assembled from spare parts—one ear up, one down, coat of no particular color. The dog looked at me with what I can only call recognition, though we'd never met. Maybe it was the sitting. The being still in a world that moves. The dog would not be hurried, and the man stopped, and we talked about nothing, and then they continued around the corner, and I never learned either of their names, and this is the way most encounters go, these brief intersections that don't accumulate into narrative but somehow still matter, still deposit something in the sediment of who we become.

I used to want everything to mean something. The career, the trajectory, the coherent story you tell at reunions. Now I suspect meaning is more like the buttons—accumulated, disordered, occasionally useful but mostly just present, witnesses to the fact that you were here, you fastened things against the wind, you came undone and were refastened or not, you persisted in your form.

The word *persists* keeps coming. I think it's because I'm tired of the language of transformation, the imperative to become, to optimize, to shed your skin like it's a moral failing to keep any of it. I want to honor the skin. The callus on my right middle finger from holding pens wrong since I was six. The scar on my knee from a bicycle I don't remember the color of. The way I still startle at loud noises, still want to be chosen first in games I no longer play, still wake sometimes at 3 AM with the specific dread that I have forgotten something important and it's too late to recover it.

What if nothing is recovered? What if everything important is precisely what we don't retain, what leaks through the fingers of attention, what we weren't even aware we were learning? My grandmother never taught me to sew. I don't know her recipe for the cookies I remember tasting. But I know the sound of buttons, the patience of her hands, the way she said my name like it was a complete sentence. I know that love can be a jar of objects without order, waiting.

The light has moved. It's 7:23 now, and the dust motes have shifted to a different quadrant of the room, and I'm breathing regularly, and somewhere a dog is walking with a person who doesn't hurry it, and a tree is either growing or it isn't, and the cells of my body are quietly replacing themselves while I sit here, becoming someone who will still shake a jar of buttons and hear her, still sit on curbs and talk to strangers, still hold my breath for no reason and then release it, release it, release it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The morning light hit the windowsill differently that Tuesday, and I noticed because I'd stopped noticing for three years. That's how it works, isn't it? The things you see every day become invisible until something cracks, and then you see everything. The dust. The way the paint peels exactly where your thumb rests when you close the cabinet. The neighbor's dog that barks at 6:47, not 6:45, and you've been wrong about it for months.

I used to collect rocks as a child. Not interesting rocks—just rocks. Gray ones from the driveway, reddish ones from the elementary school playground, a white one I convinced myself was a fossil because it had a stripe. My mother threw them out during a move, and I cried for an hour, which seems excessive now, but I was mourning something I couldn't name. The weight of them in my pockets. The way they grounded me when the world felt too fast, too loud, too full of people expecting me to be someone I hadn't figured out how to be yet.

My grandmother spoke to her plants. Not in a whimsical way, not "grow big and strong" nonsense. She told them about her day. "Mrs. Henderson asked me to make three pies for the church auction and I said yes because I can't say no, and now my hands hurt already thinking about it." The plants never answered, which was perhaps the point. She died with a fern on her hospital nightstand, and I wondered later if anyone thought to water it, if it died too, if someone threw it out with the get-well balloons.

I've been thinking about inheritance. Not money. The other things. The way my father clears his throat before he says something difficult, which I do now. The recipe for potato soup that isn't written anywhere but lives in my hands, muscle memory of how much milk, when the potatoes are soft enough. The fear of open water. The particular angle of my mother's handwriting, which I copied so obsessively in sixth grade that now mine is indistinguishable from hers, and sometimes I can't remember which of us wrote a note.

Time is a liar. It tells you that the difficult thing you're doing is permanent, that you'll always feel this tired, this uncertain, this quietly desperate in grocery store parking lots. Then it tells you that the good thing was fleeting, that you should have paid better attention, that you'll never feel that particular joy again. Both are true and neither are true, and the trick is holding both without letting them crush you flat.

I met a man once who'd walked across Spain. The Camino, though he didn't call it that, just "the walk." He said the hardest part was the flat stretches, not the mountains. "Your mind needs the struggle," he told me, drinking coffee I hadn't asked to buy him. "When it's easy, you remember why you're walking, and sometimes that's worse than blisters." I thought he was being dramatic, the way people are about things they've done that they need to matter. But I remember it now, the flat stretches, the days when nothing happens and that's somehow unbearable.

We don't talk enough about maintenance. The work of keeping things going. Marriage, yes, but also: the furnace filter, the friendship you have to keep choosing, the body that needs more sleep than you want to give it, the creative practice that feels pointless on the bad days. Everyone celebrates starting. The new job, the first date, the blank page. No one throws a party for the third year of something, the ordinary Tuesday when you do it again because you said you would, and saying you would matters even when the doing feels small.

I read once that the human brain can't distinguish between physical and social pain, that rejection activates the same regions as a broken arm. I don't know if that's true, but I know that some goodbyes still ache in my body years later, specific locations I could point to. The stomach, mostly. The chest. The place behind my eyes that hurts when I'm trying not to cry in public, which happens more than I'd like to admit, because I cry at commercials, at old people holding hands, at the particular slant of autumn light through yellow leaves that means something is ending and I don't know how to hold the beauty and the grief together.

The last time I saw my childhood home, someone else lived there. They'd painted the door red, which looked wrong, though I couldn't say why. The tree I'd climbed was gone, not even a stump. I stood in the street for too long, and a woman came out and asked if I needed help, and I couldn't explain that I was haunting my own life, that I was a ghost in a place that had stopped being mine without asking permission. She looked concerned. I left. I think about that door sometimes, how red it was, how final.

There's a theory I like, probably unscientific, that we leave pieces of ourselves in places we've been, that a version of you still exists in every room you ever loved, every car that carried you somewhere important, every corner of the world where you were changed. I hope that's true. I hope there's a version of me still in my grandmother's kitchen, learning to roll pie crust, still in the passenger seat of my best friend's car at seventeen, singing too loud with the windows down, still on a beach in Oregon watching my dog run in circles because the sand was new and everything was possible. I hope they're happy, those versions. I hope they know I'm still here, carrying them, trying to be worth what they believed.

I'm running out of words, and I haven't said anything important, not really. But maybe that's the point. The unimportant things are what stay. The way your coffee tastes on a normal morning. The specific sound of someone you love coming home. The rocks in your pocket, heavy and real, grounding you in a world that keeps spinning, indifferent and beautiful, terrible and brief, yours while you have it, which is never long enough, which is always, somehow, exactly long enough.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The morning light hit the windowsill at exactly 6:47, which meant Mrs. Chen was already three minutes late opening her bakery. I watched from my apartment across the street, coffee growing cold, as she hurried through the alley with her gray bun coming undone. She always wore the same canvas coat, the one with flour permanently ground into the cuffs. I'd never bought anything from her. I just liked knowing she existed.

My grandmother believed that objects absorb the intentions of their makers. She would hold a spoon and tell you if the person who forged it had been angry, if the wood had been carved by patient hands. I inherited this useless talent, or curse, or whatever you want to call it. The laptop I'm typing on carries a low-grade anxiety, forty workers' worth, assembled somewhere I can't picture clearly. My grandmother would have wept for three days touching this keyboard.

I think about her when I buy secondhand furniture. The dresser in my bedroom came from an estate sale in Montclair. Heavy oak, 1920s, dovetail joints that will outlast the species that made them. It hums with satisfaction. Whoever built it took their time, was paid fairly, went home to a house that smelled of something cooking. The previous owner, the one who died, she left behind a different feeling—loneliness, but the soft kind, not desperate. A loneliness of choice, of long widowhood, of evenings with the radio and a single glass of wine. I sleep better knowing she was basically okay.

The worst thing I ever touched was a child's drawing, framed, at another estate sale. The mother had kept it for sixty years. The crayon lines were frantic, violent, the paper torn in places from pressure. I dropped it and walked out. Some things aren't meant to be preserved. Some love is just damage with good branding.

I've been thinking about the word "whatever" in your prompt. It's a shield word, a deflection. "Write whatever" means "I don't want to limit you" but also "I don't want to be responsible for what you produce." Fair enough. I don't want to be responsible either. But here we are, two people connected by a screen and a request, and I'm choosing to tell you about Mrs. Chen and my grandmother and a child's drawing that still haunts me, while somewhere an algorithm is predicting what I'll say next and getting it wrong, because the algorithm doesn't know about the flour in Mrs. Chen's cuffs or the way grief can be soft and sustained or how I once loved someone who collected vintage maps and would spread them across our bed like we were planning voyages we'd never take.

We broke up because she wanted to go on the voyages and I wanted to keep planning them. That's reductive. The truth is she wanted to feel the ocean and I wanted to feel the possibility of ocean, the word *atlantic* in a copperplate font, the dotted line of a route that could still change. She was right to leave. I was wrong to let her.

I have 847 words left and the pressure of that number is suddenly enormous. What deserves to be included? The scar on my left knee from falling off a bike at eleven, how I still remember the exact color of the gravel? The way my father pronounced "library" without the first R, a working-class marker he tried to lose and I tried to keep? The dream I had last week where I could breathe underwater but chose not to, just stood on the ocean floor watching fish ignore me?

I read once that fish don't have eyelids because they don't need to blink in water. I think about this constantly. The constant exposure, the inability to close yourself off even for a second. No wonder we invented dry land, houses, curtains, the whole architecture of interruption. No wonder we invented "how are you" as something to say instead of something to mean.

Mrs. Chen is selling mooncakes now. It's September, almost the festival. I can see the red boxes through her window, the gold characters I can't read. She has a granddaughter who helps on weekends, a teenager with dyed blue hair who treats the customers with the perfect balance of efficiency and barely concealed contempt. I love her for this. I love the continuity of it, the grandmother and the granddaughter, the flour and the attitude, the old country and the new, all of it surviving in a storefront that will be a Starbucks in five years, probably, because the rent is going up and up and the city doesn't actually want the people who make it a city, just the people who can afford to visit the idea of one.

I'm down to 612 words and I want to use them to apologize for being bleak, but I'm not going to. The bleakness is accurate. The bleakness is the weather, not the climate. Underneath it, Mrs. Chen still opens her shop, the granddaughter still rolls her eyes, someone is still building dressers that will outlast the trees. My grandmother is still dead but her strange gift persists in me, useless, unasked-for, occasionally beautiful when I find the right object, the right hands, the right intention made solid.

I touched a violin once in a pawn shop. It was cheap, mass-produced, probably worth less than the case. But someone had played it for years, someone with no better instrument who still needed the sound. It held longing like a held note, sustained past the point of breath. I bought it and gave it to a school music program. I don't know if any child plays it now. I don't want to know. The transfer is what mattered, the passing of that longing into new hands, new lungs, new possible futures.

The word "whatever" also means "no matter what." Whatever comes to me, no matter what, I will write. That's braver than it sounds. Most of what comes to me is mundane, repetitive, the mental equivalent of Mrs. Chen's flour, ground into everything. But sometimes there's the violin. Sometimes there's the underwater dream. Sometimes there's the memory of being eleven and falling, the gravel in my knee, my father running toward me with an expression I couldn't read then but now understand was terror held in check by the necessity of appearing calm, of being the person who would fix this, who would always fix this, who would one day be fixed in memory as someone who tried, who ran, who arrived out of breath and scooped me up regardless of the blood, the gravel, the screaming that must have been mine but felt like it came from everywhere at once.

I have 378 words and I want to tell you about the time I saw a hawk catch a pigeon in mid-air, the explosion of feathers, the sudden silence of the other pigeons, the hawk landing on a fire escape with its prey still alive, still looking around with that particular pigeon confusion, not yet understanding that the story was over. I was late to work because I couldn't stop watching. I was late because I needed to see the end, and the end took longer than I expected, the pigeon taking its time dying, the hawk taking its time starting, and both of them in no hurry because what is hurry when you are exactly where you are meant to be, predator and prey, the most honest relationship, no flour, no grief, no underwater dreams, just the fact of hunger and the fact of being food, which is also a kind of purpose, a kind of being chosen.

I don't know why I'm telling you this. I don't know why anyone tells anyone anything. The words accumulate, the stories accumulate, and we hope someone will sort them when we're gone, or we hope no one will, that we'll dissolve like the pigeon, become something else, feed something else, not be a story at all but just energy, just matter, just the endless recycling that makes it possible for Mrs. Chen to exist across from me, for her granddaughter to exist, for the mooncakes to exist in their red and gold boxes, for your prompt to exist and my response to exist and for you, whoever you are, to be reading this now, perhaps bored, perhaps patient, perhaps also watching someone across a street, wondering about their life, their flour, their grief, their particular way of continuing.

203 words. I should use them to end something. But nothing ends, not really. The hawk is still on the fire escape in my memory. The pigeon is still dying. My father is still running. My grandmother is still holding a spoon and weeping for workers she never met. The algorithm is still predicting and failing. Mrs. Chen is still three minutes late, always three minutes late, her bun coming undone, her canvas coat floured, her shop opening into the morning that keeps arriving regardless of what we write or don't write, want or don't want, understand or fail to understand.

Whatever comes to me. Whatever comes to you. The words run out but the world doesn't. The world never does.

The morning light hits different when you haven't slept. Not better, not worse—just *different*. Like the world is a photograph slightly overexposed, edges bleeding into other edges, everything too honest, too there.

I keep thinking about my grandmother's hands. She made bread every Thursday until she was eighty-three. The rhythm of it: punch, fold, rest, repeat. A language she spoke without knowing she was fluent. I tried once. The dough came out dense as a failed metaphor, heavy with intention rather than air. She laughed and said yeast was patient but not stupid. I still don't know what she meant. I think that's the point.

There's a cat in my neighborhood who sits on the same fence post at 4:47 PM, give or take four minutes. I've timed it. I don't know its name. I don't know if it has a home, or if the fence post *is* the home, a vertical territory claimed against the chaos of lawns and garbage days and dogs. Sometimes I bring it treats. Sometimes I forget for weeks. It doesn't seem to mind either way. This is the relationship I've cultivated most successfully in three years.

My friend died in March. Not COVID. Something quieter, more cellular, a rebellion of his own blood that no one expected because he was the healthy one, the runner, the non-smoker, the joke. I keep wanting to text him about the cat. About the bread. About how I finally understand that "yeast was patient but not stupid" means you can't force things to rise by wanting them to. You can only create conditions and wait. He would have argued with me. He would have said something about thermodynamics or free will or how my grandmother was probably just making fun of me. I would have laughed. I'm not laughing now. The text sits in my drafts. The drafts sit in me.

I read somewhere that humans can only maintain about 150 meaningful social connections. Dunbar's number. The rest are acquaintances, context, noise. I think about this when I'm in the grocery store, surrounded by faces I'll never know, each carrying their own fence posts, their own dead friends, their own Thursday bread rituals. The loneliness of that number. The relief of it too. Permission to not know everyone. Permission to be unknown.

The word *whatever* in your prompt is doing heavy lifting. It's a shrug and an invitation. It's the linguistic equivalent of leaving a door unlocked. I appreciate it. Most prompts want something specific—my trauma, my expertise, my polished little insight. This just asks for *whatever comes*. What comes is rarely polished. What comes is the cat, the hands, the dead friend, the number 150 floating like a balloon I can't tell if I should catch or release.

I used to write poetry. Bad poetry, mostly, but sincere. The kind where every line break was a gasp and every metaphor mixed until it was barely breathing. I stopped because sincerity started to feel embarrassing. Then I started again because embarrassment started to feel like a small price for being in the world without a mask. Then I stopped again because the world got so loud that sincerity felt like shouting into a hurricane. Now I write this. Whatever this is. Prose that wants to be poetry that wants to be a conversation that wants to be silence.

Silence is underrated. My apartment has a particular silence at 2 AM that I would recognize blindfolded. It's not empty silence. It's *full*—of the refrigerator's hum, the distant highway, my own blood moving through my ears like a tide I can't control. Sometimes I sit in it and try to hear the cat on the fence post, three miles away, not making a sound. I never can. But I try. The trying is its own sound.

My grandmother died before my friend. Pneumonia, the old enemy, the final punch and fold. She never saw my bread improve, which is probably merciful. I make decent bread now. Not great. The crust cracks right, the crumb has some give. I don't make it on Thursdays. That day is hers, still, even in absence. I make it on Tuesdays, which feels appropriately unpoetic, a day that belongs to no one, a day that waits without expectation.

The cat doesn't know I'm writing about it. This is the fundamental condition of being written about: ignorance, or at least the inability to consent. I wonder what would change if the cat knew. Would it choose a different fence post? Would it look at me differently, with the weight of representation? Probably not. Cats are good at refusing metaphor. They just *are*, which is a kind of wisdom I circle around but never land on.

I have 647 words left. The counting is part of the exercise, a frame that both contains and reveals. Without the limit, I might drift forever. With it, I have to choose. The cat or the bread. The friend or the grandmother. The silence or the sound of trying to hear silence. I choose all of them, which is cheating, but life cheats too. It gives you multiple things to mourn, multiple things to notice, multiple fence posts to claim at 4:47 PM with your particular shadow.

Someone is playing piano in the building next door. Badly, beautifully, the same four measures of something classical I can't name. They've been playing it for twenty minutes. I want to knock on the wall and ask them to finish, or to start something else, or to tell me what it is. I won't. The not-knowing is part of the music now. The repetition is its own composition. I think of my grandmother's hands again, the way she'd start a song on the piano she never finished learning, the same eight bars, the same pleasure in partial mastery.

I don't believe in afterlives. I believe in after-*effects*. The way a body moves through a room after someone has left it. The way a recipe survives the hands that made it. The way a four-measure piano piece haunts a wall. The way 1000 words contain more than their number, the way you reading this are completing something I started without knowing where it would go.

Where it went: here. To the cat, still on the post, still not knowing. To the bread, still rising on Tuesdays, still not great. To the friend, still in drafts, still not sent, still somehow sent in the writing of this. To the number 150, which I've exceeded in words if not in connections. To you, whoever you are, reading this in whatever light, whatever morning, whatever sleepless overexposure.

The piano stopped. Or I stopped hearing it. Same thing, sometimes.

I have 234 words left. I want to use them slowly. I want to make them last like the final sips of water on a hike, like the last page of a book you don't want to end, like the last conversation with someone you didn't know was leaving. The limit is a gift. It forces an ending. Real life doesn't force endings; it just continues until it doesn't, and you don't always get to know which conversation was the last, which bread was the final lesson, which 4:47 PM was the cat's last appearance on the post.

I hope the cat is still there. I hope the piano starts again. I hope my grandmother, in whatever after-effect she inhabits, has found a Thursday kitchen and hands that remember her rhythm. I hope my friend, in whatever draft he exists in now, has received the text I finally sent, the one that says *the bread rose, you would have argued, I would have laughed, I am not laughing, I am here, the cat is here, whatever comes comes*.

The morning light is changing. The overexposure is settling into something ordinary, something I can look at without flinching. This is how most things end: not with drama, but with adjustment. The eyes adapt. The heart adapts slower. The words adapt to their container, 1000 of them, now almost spent, now almost something that can be held in two hands like a loaf, like a cat that finally lets you lift it, briefly, before it returns to its post, its patience, its perfect stupid beautiful refusal to be anything other than exactly what it is.

I have 31 words left. I will use them to say: the post is warm from sun. The cat is warm from post. I am warm from writing this. You are warm from reading. Whatever comes next comes next.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The morning light hits different when you haven't slept. Not better, not worse—just *different*, like the world has been translated into a language you half-remember from childhood. I keep thinking about my grandmother's hands, the way they moved through dough without looking, muscle memory deeper than thought. She'd hum something tuneless, something that predated her own birth probably, passed down through women who never wrote anything down because who had paper, who had time, who had the belief that anyone would care to read it later.

I care now. I care so much it feels like a haunting.

There's a particular silence in libraries that isn't silence at all. It's the accumulation of thousands of pages turning in unison, the held breath of concentration, the creak of wooden shelves adjusting to humidity. I used to hide in them. Still do, when the outside gets too loud with its demands. The books don't want anything from you except attention, and even that is voluntary, a gift you give and can take back whenever you need to look out the window at a pigeon doing something inexplicable on a ledge.

I saw a man crying on the bus once. Not quietly, not the dignified single tear of cinema. Ugly crying, the kind that makes your face red and your nose run and your whole body shake with the effort of keeping itself together. Nobody looked. This is the unspoken contract of public transit: we will carry you forward, but we will not witness you. I broke the contract. I handed him a packet of tissues I'd been carrying for months. He took it without meeting my eyes, and I understood that this was the better kindness—not making him be seen, just making him be *helped*.

The tissues were from a hotel in Prague. I stole them because they had the hotel's name embossed in gold and I thought, *who does this, who makes tissues fancy*, and then I kept them because they were fancy, because sometimes you need to remember that ordinary things can be made special by effort and intention. The man on the bus blew his nose into Prague. I hope it helped.

I want to talk about water. Everyone does, eventually. We're mostly made of it, we search for it on other planets as if that would mean something definitive, we watch it destroy and create with the same indifferent power. I grew up near a lake that was technically a reservoir, man-made, which always disappointed me. I wanted natural grandeur, not municipal planning. But the fish didn't know the difference. The herons that stood still as meditation didn't file complaints about authenticity. Water finds its level, that's the phrase, and I think about that constantly—how we are all finding our level, sometimes slowly, sometimes in floods that take out everything we thought was permanent.

My level seems to be restlessness. I am never quite where I am, always planning the next, mourning the last, missing the present like a train I've run for and still somehow missed. The Buddhists would have a field day with me. Or maybe they wouldn't; maybe they'd just sit with me in the missing, not trying to fix it, because fixing is another kind of running.

I ran a marathon once. Never again. The human body was not meant to do this, I decided at mile twenty, my knees making sounds that belonged in a horror film trailer. But the finish line—someone had written "YOU ARE LOVED" on the pavement in chalk, and I stepped on it without meaning to, and I cried in a way that was different from the bus man, a release rather than a breaking, and a stranger hugged me, sweaty and salt-crusted and real in a way that most interactions never are. We never spoke. I don't know her name. I hope she's loved too, hope someone writes it for her when she needs to step on it.

The word "liminal" has been overused lately, but I don't care. I love it. I love the spaces between, the thresholds, the hours after a party ends and before sleep comes, the airport at 3 AM where everyone is suspended between where they were and where they're going, no longer citizens of either place. These are honest spaces. They don't pretend to be destinations. We need more honesty about the in-between, I think. We sell each other so many finish lines, so many arrivals, and then wonder why everyone feels cheated when the feeling of arrival dissipates, as it always does, as it must, because arrival is just the beginning of another departure if you're doing it right.

I'm doing it wrong a lot of the time. I hold onto arrivals like they owe me something. I want the party to last forever, the book to never end, the conversation to continue looping back on itself so we never have to say goodnight and face the separate silence of our separate rooms. But the book ends, and the party, and the conversation, and the silence is where I meet myself, where I have to decide if I'm company worth keeping.

Sometimes yes. Sometimes I make myself tea and read something that makes me feel less alone with my particular strangeness, and the silence becomes not empty but full, a held note rather than an absence. Sometimes no. Sometimes I scroll until my thumb hurts, avoiding the mirror, avoiding the questions that wait like patient predators. The tea gets cold. The book stays closed. I am not good company on these nights, and I know it, and I stay anyway, because leaving myself would mean going where?

There's a story I half-remember about a man who learned to be invisible. Not literally—this isn't that kind of story. He just stopped making noise, stopped taking up space, stopped wanting things that would require him to be seen. He became so good at it that he started to forget himself, would walk past mirrors without recognition, would feel surprised when someone bumped into him because he'd forgotten he had mass, occupied volume, existed in the same way tables and doorframes existed. The story ends with him trying to become visible again and failing, or maybe succeeding but finding it painful, too bright, too loud. I can't remember which ending I read, or if both exist and I chose one without knowing I was choosing.

I think about him when I feel myself disappearing. When I say "fine" too many times and mean it too little. When I agree to things I don't want because wanting feels like a risk, and not-wanting feels like a kind of death but a quiet one, a death you can almost pretend is just rest. The trick is to catch yourself mid-fade, to do something deliberate and slightly too loud, to remind yourself and others that you are here, you take up space, you have mass and volume and the right to both.

I bought a bright orange coat last winter. This was my deliberate act. I who had worn black and gray and the colors of intentional obscurity for years, I who had wanted to be a shadow that helpful people didn't bump into. The orange coat made people look. Made them smile sometimes, or comment, or just register my presence in a way that felt at first like exposure, like standing naked in a dream, and later like relief, like remembering you have a body and it can be warm, it can be seen, it can be *chosen*.

I choose the orange coat even when I don't feel like being chosen. Especially then. The discipline of visibility, the practice of presence. It's not natural to me, will never be natural, but it's becoming possible, becoming something I can reach for when I feel the familiar comfort of fading calling me back to invisibility, to the story with the ending I don't want.

What else? The thousand words are running down and I want to spend them all, want to leave nothing in reserve, because what is reserve but another kind of holding back, another small disappearance? I want to tell you about the time I heard a child explain to another child that the moon follows you because it likes you, and how I believed her instantly, wanted to believe, needed to believe that something in the sky could be that personal, that attentive, that *kind*. I want to tell you about my neighbor who plays saxophone badly at 7 PM every evening, the same three songs, and how I've come to love the badness, the trying, the refusal to be good enough as a reason to stop. I want to tell you about the smell of rain on hot pavement, which scientists have named but which I prefer to think of as unnamed, as private, as belonging to everyone who has ever stood in it and felt suddenly, inexplicably, *hope*.

Hope is harder than despair. Despair has gravity, pulls you down with the certainty of falling. Hope requires you to lift, to push against the weight, to believe in the possibility of flight without any evidence of wings. I am learning to hope like I learned to wear orange—not naturally, not easily, but deliberately, with the understanding that the effort is part of the point, that choosing to hope is itself a kind of hope, a refusal to let the last word be the one that ends the story.

The story doesn't end. That's the secret I want to leave you with, the one I'm still learning, the one that keeps me writing past the point where I thought I'd stop. The bus man is somewhere now, maybe still crying, maybe not. The marathon stranger is living a life I'll never know. The invisible man is still trying to be seen, or has succeeded, or has become a story that someone else will half-remember and use to understand their own fading. It doesn't end. It keeps going, liminal and present and hopeful and visible, and we are in it, we are part of it, we are here.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The morning light hit the kitchen counter at exactly the wrong angle, and I realized I'd been measuring my life in coffee rings and the particular silence of a house where no one else was awake yet. There's a geometry to loneliness that no one teaches you—the way it fills corners first, pools in the spaces between furniture, climbs the walls like a slow tide.

I used to think memory worked like a filing cabinet. Now I know it's more like a garden that refuses to be planned. The tomatoes volunteer where the roses should be. The compost of old embarrassments heats up without warning, steaming in the cold dawn. I am forty-three years old and I still wake up sometimes convinced I have a math test I haven't studied for, the anxiety so real I can smell the chalk dust, taste the metallic tang of the fountain water in that hallway with the green linoleum.

My grandmother kept a jar of buttons on her dresser. Not useful buttons, not spare ones for emergencies. These were archaeological. A mother-of-pearl disk from a coat she wore to a dance in 1957. A wooden toggle from a sweater that smelled of her husband's pipe tobacco. A bright red plastic circle from a child's coat—my mother's, I think, though the story shifted depending on the day and the light. She would run them through her fingers like worry beads, and I understand that now. The body needs something to occupy itself when the mind is busy falling through time.

I read once that the human heart can continue beating for several minutes after being removed from the chest. I don't know if this is true and I don't want to verify it. But I think about it when I'm in traffic, when the radio plays something I wasn't expecting, when the song is from a year that no longer exists except in the amber of melody. The heart doesn't know. The heart keeps going, stubborn, stupid, magnificent. It doesn't understand that the rest of the system has quit, has moved on, has become something else.

My neighbor practices saxophone on Tuesday evenings. He's not good. He may never be good. But there's something in the reaching that matters, in the sound of someone trying to bend air into meaning. I sit on my porch and listen to him wrestle with "Blue Moon" and I want to tell him that perfection is the enemy of the actual, that the cracked notes are where the light gets in, but we don't have that kind of relationship. We have the kind where we nod at the mailboxes, where we comment on the weather with the sincerity of people who have nothing else to say and find that, somehow, it is enough.

The cat sleeps in a patch of sun that moves across the floor like a clock made of warmth. I have never been as committed to anything as she is to this migration, this following of light across the hours. She does not check her phone. She does not wonder if she should be doing something else, something more productive, more aligned with her goals. She is fully in the sun, and then the sun moves, and she moves with it. There is no story she tells herself about this. There is only the warmth, and then the seeking of warmth.

I am tired of the word "journey." I am tired of the word "authentic." I want a language that hasn't been focus-grouped, that doesn't come with a hashtag attached. I want to describe the feeling of finding a photograph of yourself as a child and not recognizing the eyes, the particular hope in them that you have somehow lost without noticing, like a sweater left on a bus. What is the word for that? We don't have it. We have "nostalgia," which is too sweet, too much like candy. What I feel is more like archaeology. More like digging through layers and finding evidence of a civilization that used the same name I use but was otherwise incomprehensible.

Last week I found a grocery list in a used book. *Milk. Eggs. Call Sarah. Band-Aids. Something for the garden.* I kept it. I don't know why. Maybe because it was proof that someone else was trying to hold things together with paper and ink, that the ordinary emergencies of being alive don't require heroic language, just a list, just the next small thing. Call Sarah. What happened when Sarah was called? I'll never know. The book was a novel about a man who builds a boat in his attic, which is impossible, which is the point. The boat is never finished. The man dies with sawdust in his hair and the attic door nailed shut by his children, who don't understand, who think he was crazy.

But he wasn't crazy. He was building a boat. In the wrong place, with the wrong tools, for a sea that didn't exist. And isn't that what we're all doing, in our different attics, with our different impossible materials? The boat is not the point. The building is the point. The sawdust in the hair. The refusal to stop even when the dimensions are wrong, even when the water never comes.

The coffee is cold now. The light has moved past the counter, into the living room, where it illuminates the dust I keep meaning to address. I will not address it today. Today I will do something else, something equally small and equally important, something that will not appear in any account of my life but without which the whole structure would collapse. I will buy milk. I will call someone, though not Sarah, who is a stranger and probably doesn't want to hear from me. I will run my fingers through buttons I don't remember acquiring. I will listen to bad saxophone and think about boats in attics, about hearts that beat in empty spaces, about the stubborn, beautiful, useless persistence of trying to make something where nothing was before.

The cat has moved. The sun has moved. I will move too, eventually, when the coffee is gone, when the list is made, when the next small thing presents itself and I answer, as I always do, as I will until I can't, with yes, with now, with this.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The morning light hit the windowsill at exactly 6:47, and Eleanor noticed because she had been waiting for it. Not consciously, perhaps, but some part of her had counted the minutes since 4:15 when she woke to the sound of a neighbor's car starting in the cold. She did not know the neighbor. She had never spoken to them in six years of shared driveway. This was the kind of detail that would have depressed her mother, who believed in casseroles and borrowing sugar, but Eleanor found it comforting. The not-knowing. The small boundaries that held.

She made coffee with the ritual she had developed in the months since David left. First the filter, folded along the seam so it fit the basket without bunching. Then three scoops of the dark roast she ordered online from a roaster in Portland, though she had never been to Portland and could not picture it accurately. She imagined it always with too many bridges, too much rain, not enough of whatever made a city knowable. The water had to be just off boiling. She had read this somewhere and now could not deviate. The coffee was never quite right anyway, always a little bitter, always a little thin. She drank it black at the kitchen table, watching the light move across the worn pine surface in patterns she had memorized without meaning to.

The cat appeared at 7:12, jumping onto the chair opposite hers with the entitlement of animals who have never been refused. He was orange, getting old, named after a poet she no longer read. "Milton," she said, not really addressing him, and he ignored her, which was the correct response. She had found him in the garage eleven years ago, half-feral, eating something she did not examine. Now he was fat and demanding and the only living thing that slept in her bed. She did not think about what this meant. She had stopped thinking about what things meant as a general practice, finding that meaning accumulated too quickly, became too heavy to carry through ordinary days.

By 8:30 she was dressed, though this was a generous term for the arrangement of garments she had settled into. Loose pants, a sweater that had been her mother's, shoes she could stand in for hours. She worked at the library three days a week, shelving and repairing, the kind of work that left her hands rough and her mind mercifully empty. Today was not a work day. Today was Tuesday, which meant the grocery store, the post office, the careful navigation of errands that could be completed before noon, before the parking lots filled with people who had somewhere to be in the afternoon.

The grocery store was two miles away, and she drove through streets she had stopped seeing. The same houses, the same seasonal decorations, the same dog walker with three mismatched dogs who always seemed slightly desperate. She parked in the same spot when she could, near the cart return, and took a list she had written on the back of an envelope. Bread. Milk. The apples she ate every afternoon at 3:00. She did not vary her diet. This was not discipline but exhaustion, the inability to imagine wanting something different from what she had wanted yesterday.

In the produce section, she encountered a man looking at the oranges with the intensity of someone defusing a bomb. She knew this intensity. She had brought it to the selection of tomatoes, of yogurt, of all the small decisions that composed a life when the large decisions had already been made or unmade. She moved past him, reached for her apples, and heard him say "excuse me" in a voice that was not asking to be excused but announcing himself.

"Do you know if these are blood oranges?" he asked, holding up a piece of fruit that was clearly, obviously a blood orange, the dark rind unmistakable.

"Yes," she said. "They are."

"I thought so," he said, not putting it down. "I just wanted to be sure."

She nodded and moved away, but he followed her, or seemed to, appearing at the cheese case, the bread aisle, always with a question that was not quite a question. Had she tried the sourdough? Did she know if the store carried fresh mozzarella on Tuesdays? She answered with the minimum required, polite, final, and eventually he stopped appearing, or she stopped noticing, which was the same thing in the geometry of grocery stores.

At home, she put everything away in the same places. The apples in the bowl on the counter, the bread in the bread box her mother had given her as a wedding gift, back when people gave wedding gifts and she had been someone who received them. She ate lunch standing at the counter, crackers and the cheese she had not wanted to discuss, and then she sat in the chair by the window with a book she had read before, many times, a book she could enter without the risk of surprise.

The afternoon passed in its usual manner. The light moved. The cat shifted positions. She read the same paragraph three times and did not mind, having learned that reading was not always about progression, sometimes it was about the holding of a thought, the turning of it in the mind like a stone in the palm. At 3:00 she ate an apple. At 4:30 she made tea. These were the events of the day, and she did not wish for others, or if she did, the wish was so buried she could not excavate it without tools she no longer possessed.

But something happened at 5:47, or rather she noticed something that had been happening without her attention. The light on the windowsill, which she had observed that morning with the patience of someone waiting for nothing, had returned to the same position, the same angle, the same quality of gold that seemed to come from somewhere else, not the sun but the idea of the sun, the memory of it held in the glass and the dust and the particular silence of her kitchen. She watched it for longer than she had watched anything in months, longer than the man with the oranges, longer than the cat's various sleeps, longer than her own grief which she had measured in days and then weeks and then stopped measuring because the units had become too large to manage.

She thought of David, which she tried not to do at specific times, having learned that scheduled grief was worse than accidental grief, more concentrated, more poisonous. But she thought of him now without the usual compression in her chest, the usual sense of something falling that would not stop falling. She thought of him making coffee in this same kitchen, not with her ritual but with his chaos, grounds on the counter, water too hot or too cold, the result always acceptable to him because he did not taste things the way she did, did not experience the world as a series of precise sensations that could be wrong. He had left because she was precise, because she could not stop being precise, because love had become for her a kind of measurement and he had failed to measure up or she had failed to measure him generously, she was never sure which, the failure was mutual, the failure was the air they had breathed together until they could not breathe it anymore.

The light moved. She watched it move. And she felt something that was not happiness, was not even relief, but was perhaps the space where happiness or relief might eventually grow, the cleared ground, the possibility of planting. She did not know what she would plant. She did not know if she had seeds, if she knew how to tend anything that required more than water and the occasional word. But the light was there, and she was there, and the cat was there, and the man with the oranges was somewhere in the world with his uncertainty and his need to confirm what he already knew, and all of this seemed suddenly, briefly, enough to constitute a life, not the life she had planned or failed to plan, but a life that was continuing without her full participation, that would continue, that asked only that she remain present for it, that she watch the light move and move with it, that she allow the hours to accumulate in their small, unremarkable ways, that she trust the pattern she could not yet see but could, perhaps, begin to imagine.

She made dinner. She ate it. She read until her eyes grew heavy, and then she slept, and in the morning the light returned to the windowsill at 6:47, and she was there to meet it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The morning light hit the kitchen counter at an angle that made the dust visible, each particle suspended in its own slow orbit, and I thought about how we are all just dust that learned to complain. My grandmother's ceramic rooster watched from the windowsill, beak eternally open in a crow he would never finish. She bought it in 1987 from a man who swore it was hand-painted in Portugal. It was made in Ohio. The lie outlived her.

I've been thinking about the physics of regret. How it doesn't dissipate like heat but accumulates, mass without volume, until you're carrying a black hole in your ribcage that weighs precisely nothing and everything. Last Tuesday I saw a man at the bus stop reading a manual for a refrigerator he'd owned for twelve years. "Finally getting around to it," he said, though I hadn't asked. The manual was in German. He didn't speak German. This is what we do with instructions we never requested.

My neighbor waters her concrete driveway every evening at six. She believes this prevents cracks. The water runs into the street, down the grate, joins the river, the ocean, the clouds, falls again on some other driveway where someone else stands with a hose, believing they are holding back entropy with a green rubber grip. We are all Sisyphus but with worse posture and no mythic significance.

The word "sillage" refers to the scent-trail left by perfume. I learned this from a woman who left my apartment at 4 AM and took all the warmth with her. For weeks I would enter rooms and still smell her decision to go. The dictionary calls it a wake, like behind a boat, like after a death. We have so few words for departure that we must recycle them until they mean everything and nothing, like "love" or "okay" or "I'm fine."

Children are born with about 100 more bones than adults have. They fuse, ossify, become rigid with time. We are born flexible and spend our lives becoming architecture. I think about this when I see toddlers fold themselves into spaces that shouldn't accommodate them, when I try to touch my toes and my body sends back a polite refusal, a returned letter, address unknown.

There is a town in Japan where they make fake food for restaurant displays. The craftsmen study real food for hours, then reproduce it in resin and wax. The shrimp tempura will never cool. The lettuce will never wilt. The perfect meal, eternally almost-ready. I want to ask them if they dream of hunger, if the imitation of satisfaction becomes its own kind of nourishment. I never go to Japan. I look at pictures online and feel approximately informed.

My father kept a list of every book he read from 1974 to 2003. The handwriting changed, tightened, then loosened again when arthritis arrived. Somewhere around 1987 the titles stop being things he chose and start being things assigned, recommended, expected. You can see the exact moment he stopped reading for pleasure and started reading for proof that he was still the kind of person who read. The list ends mid-page. I don't know if he stopped keeping it or stopped reading or just stopped needing evidence.

The Voyager golden record contains a heartbeat. Ann Druyan's, recorded while she thought about Carl Sagan, whom she would later marry. The sound of love traveling at 35,000 miles per hour toward stars that may have already died, carrying Bach and Chuck Berry and the hope that something, somewhere, will know what a heartbeat means. We are so desperate to be understood that we launched our longing into the dark with no address, no return postage, just the assumption that beauty is a language with no need for translation.

I used to think nostalgia was a weakness. Now I think it's a survival mechanism, the brain's way of saying *this mattered* when the present insists nothing matters yet. The smell of chalkboards. The particular green of library card catalogues. The weight of a phone receiver in the crook of your neck, cord stretched to its limit so you could stand in the doorway and watch rain while someone you would eventually lose told you about their day. These details are not important. They are everything.

The last person who knew how to make Stradivari's varnish died without explaining it. We have his instruments, their sound, their impossible resonance, but not the recipe. Some knowledge travels only through bodies, dies with them, becomes archaeology of the air. I wonder what I know that I cannot explain, what will vanish when I do, what small craft I perform without understanding its mechanics, its worth.

At the hospital where I was born, they now use that wing for storage. Boxes of files no one will request. The room where my mother first held me holds fluorescent light and the smell of old paper. I want to visit it but they don't allow visitors to storage. The building remembers nothing. The building doesn't need to. The building is still standing, which is its own kind of memory, its own indifferent continuity.

I read that sharks have to keep moving to breathe. The water flows through, extracts oxygen, requires motion. To stop is to suffocate. I think about this when I can't sleep, when I scroll through feeds I don't care about, when I answer "busy" to "how are you" because stillness feels like drowning. We are all sharks in a tank too small, circling, circling, telling ourselves the motion is the point.

The word "petrichor" was invented in 1964 by two scientists who studied the smell of rain on dry earth. Before that, we had the experience but not the name. How many things do we feel that remain unnamed because the right two people haven't collaborated yet? The particular ache of seeing someone you used to know in a crowd and choosing not to say hello. The way a house sounds different when you know you're leaving it. The exact color of the light at the moment you realize you are older than your parents were when they had you.

I keep a box of letters I will never send. The recipients are scattered, dead, estranged, or simply uninterested in my versions of events. The letters grow more accurate with time, less concerned with persuasion, more with record. This is what I saw. This is what I failed to say. This is how I remember it, which is not how it was, but how it remains in the only archive I have, this faulty, loving, self-serving mind.

The oldest known melody was written on a cuneiform tablet in Syria, fourteen centuries before the common era. It was for a stringed instrument, maybe a lyre. The notation is partly understood. We can play something close to what they played, but not exact, never exact, the gap between then and now unbridgeable by any music. Still, someone plays it. Someone always plays it. The approximation of connection is itself a kind of connection, the reaching across time with imperfect hands, saying *I hear you, or something like you, or what I imagine you might have been.*

My cat sleeps sixteen hours a day and wakes without apology, without the need to justify her existence through productivity. I have never envied anything more completely. The moral of evolution is not progress but adaptation, and she has adapted to a world that provides, that asks nothing in return but presence, the occasional purr, the acknowledgment that warmth is enough, that enough is rare and sufficient.

I am running out of words now, which is the condition of all things, the built-in limit that makes them precious. The ceramic rooster still waits. The bus stop man has probably finished his manual, understood nothing, moved on to another project of incomprehension. The fake food glows in Tokyo windows. Voyager passes the edge of our influence, still singing its heart into the void. And somewhere it is raining on dry earth, making a smell that didn't have a name within my grandmother's lifetime, making it anyway, making it new each time, indifferent to whether we have words, whether we are watching, whether we will remember to move, to breathe, to continue this impossible, ordinary, sufficient motion of being alive.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The morning light hit the kitchen counter at 6:47, and I noticed for the first time that the coffee ring from yesterday had dried into something resembling a continent. Australia, maybe. Or a failed Rorschach test. I stared at it while the kettle screamed, wondering if this was how cartographers started—desperate men squinting at stains, willing borders into being.

My grandmother kept a drawer of useless things. Not junk. *Useless* things, which is different. A single earring whose mate was buried with her sister in 1987. A key to a car that rusted into a different car entirely. A photograph of a dog that, she admitted once after her third sherry, "wasn't even ours, but looked like it should have been." The drawer was her argument against the efficient universe. She never said this aloud. She didn't need to.

I think about that drawer when people ask what I do. I write, I say, which is true in the way that "I breathe" is true—technically accurate, spiritually vacant. What I actually do is collect the almost-gone. The sentence someone started in a diner booth and abandoned for their cooling eggs. The way a particular silence hangs between two people who've run out of lies but haven't found the truth yet. The coffee rings. The single earrings. The dogs that should have been ours.

---

The woman who taught me to drive was named Mrs. Patterson, and she believed the clutch was a moral test. "You're not *asking* the car," she'd say, her hand hovering near the emergency brake like a preacher near a sinner. "You're *telling* it. With your whole leg. With your intention." I failed the test twice. The third time, she wasn't there—she'd died in February, quietly, without telling anyone she was sick, which was very much her style. I passed. I still don't know if I was telling the car or asking it. I still don't know the difference.

Grief, I've learned, is not a river. It's a drawer. You open it expecting the single earring, and instead you find the key, and suddenly you're standing in your kitchen at 6:47 wondering why you're crying about a Chevrolet that dissolved into rust before you were born.

---

Last October, I found a notebook in a free library box, the kind people nail to telephone poles. It was half-filled with handwriting that started confident and deteriorated, the letters leaning like drunkards against each other. The entries were dated 2019. The owner had been tracking something they called "the project," which seemed to involve walking every street in a neighborhood I didn't recognize, noting the color of each door, whether the mail slot was brass or steel, if there was a doorbell or a knocker. Page forty-seven: "Blue. Brass. Knocker. Woman in window saw me. Did not wave."

I kept the notebook. I don't know why. I tell myself it's research, that writers are magpies, that everything shiny or strange might be useful. But the truth is simpler and more embarrassing: I wanted to know if they finished. If the woman in the window ever waved. If the project had a point, or if the point was just the walking, the noticing, the not-waving.

---

My neighbor plays saxophone at odd hours. Badly. "Blue Moon," mostly, though sometimes he attempts Coltrane and the attempt is so brave and so failed that I have to leave the apartment. Not because it's loud. Because it's *almost* something. Because I can hear the gap between what he wants and what his fingers can do, and that gap is too familiar, too full of my own almosts.

We never speak. I leave him notes when packages arrive. He once taped a bag of lemons to my door with a Post-it that said "overflow." I made lemonade that tasted like sunlight and failure. I drank it on the fire escape, watching someone three buildings over practice their own almost—ballet, I think, or maybe just stretching with ambition. The body, reaching for positions it can't hold.

---

There is a theory I read somewhere, maybe invented, that every person who has ever lived is still here in particle form, dispersed, breathed in, becoming the dust on your windowsill, the grit in your teeth. I don't believe it, but I think about it when I clean. I think: this might be Mrs. Patterson. This might be the woman in the window. This might be the almost-Coltrane, the almost-ballet, the almost-wave.

I think: we are all becoming each other's drawers. Single earrings, rusted keys, photographs of dogs that should have been ours.

---

The kettle stopped screaming. I made coffee, added the ring to Australia, decided it was maybe South America after all. The light shifted. The continent disappeared into the general brown of the counter, which is the color of so many things—dried leaves, old photographs, the particular melancholy of Tuesday mornings.

I wrote a sentence. Deleted it. Wrote another that was almost the same but different in a way I couldn't name, like the difference between asking and telling, between waving and not-waving, between the project and the walking.

The saxophone started. "Blue Moon." The bad notes, the brave notes, the gap between. I left it playing while I worked, while I collected, while I became part of someone's drawer, someone's almost, someone's morning light hitting something they didn't expect to notice.

I have 247 words left, and I don't know what to do with them. This feels important, this not-knowing. The notebook had blank pages at the end. The project, unfinished. The woman in the window, still not waving, or waving, or becoming dust, or never existing at all, just a sentence on a page, a door noted, a color named.

I could tell you something true now. I could tell you I'm afraid, that the writing doesn't get easier, that every morning is a new country drawn in coffee, unrecognized, unmapped. I could tell you I still can't drive a stick shift without hearing her voice, without asking the car, without failing the moral test. I could tell you the lemons were too sour, the lemonade was bad, I drank it anyway.

I could tell you the drawer is open. That I'm adding to it. That you're in it now, reader, whoever you are, whatever you almost became, whatever you're walking toward without knowing if it waves back.

The saxophone stopped mid-phrase. The silence that followed was not empty. It was the silence of someone putting down their instrument, looking at their fingers, deciding to try again tomorrow, or not, or to start a different project entirely, mapping new streets, new doors, new colors, new almosts.

I have 31 words.

The light moved. The counter changed. The continent was gone, or never there, or waiting to be noticed again by someone else, in some other morning, with some other kettle, some other grief that is not a river but a drawer that opens when you least expect, when you were looking for coffee, for keys, for a dog that should have been yours.

I have 7.

The woman waved.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The morning light hit the windowsill differently that Tuesday, slanting through dust motes that seemed suspended in some private conspiracy of physics. I had been thinking about my grandmother's hands, the way her knuckles swelled like tiny walnuts in her final years, how she still peeled apples with surgical precision, the red ribbon of skin falling in one continuous spiral.

Memory is not a file cabinet. It's more like a garden where things grow unexpected, where the tomato you planted in May becomes something else entirely by August, where the soil remembers floods you have forgotten. I read once that every time you recall something, you alter it slightly, like a Chinese whisper with yourself. This terrifies me and comforts me in equal measure. It means my worst days are editable. It means my best days are probably half-fabricated already.

I knew a man in Portland who kept pigeons on his roof. Not fancy breeds, just the ordinary gray kind you see in every parking lot, the ones we call flying rats. He named them all after jazz musicians. Miles would land on his shoulder and peck at his earlobe. Coltrane refused to enter the coop at night and slept on the antenna, winter and summer both. He told me pigeons can find their way home from hundreds of miles away using magnetic fields and smell, a combination of the cosmic and the mundane that seems almost too perfect, too metaphorically convenient. I didn't believe him about the names until he called out and they came, one by one, settling on the tar paper in a row like notes on a staff.

We are all of us navigating by invisible fields. The pull of childhood kitchens. The scent of someone who left. I cannot pass a certain intersection in Chicago without feeling the ghost weight of a backpack I carried at twenty-two, the specific ache of walking twelve blocks because I couldn't afford the bus, the pride and the poverty braided together so tight I still can't separate them. The brain stores emotion in the amygdala but the story of the emotion in the hippocampus, and when trauma disrupts this collaboration, you end up with fear that has no narrative, panic attacks triggered by nothing you can name. I think about this when I wake at 3 AM with my heart racing and no enemy in sight.

My friend Elena makes pottery and talks about the moment of centering, when the clay finds the middle of the wheel and suddenly everything is possible. Before that, she says, it's just fighting. The clay wins, you win, nobody wins. But centering is not something you force. You have to stop trying so hard. The clay teaches you this by failing, over and over, collapsing into wobble, becoming something you didn't plan. The best pieces, she told me, come from the salvage, the collapse that revealed something you couldn't have designed.

I have been trying to center for forty years.

The last time I saw my father, we talked about nothing important. The weather. A restaurant renovation downtown. I didn't know it was the last time. This is the banality the movies never prepare you for, how ordinary the final ordinary moments are, how you would have paid everything you own for one more conversation about nothing, one more chance to not say anything significant, to just be in the room with the person while the light did whatever it was doing, while dust motes performed their invisible choreography.

There is a word in Japanese, *aware*, for the bittersweetness of things passing. Not nostalgia, which is too self-conscious, too curated. *Aware* is the sharpness of cherry blossoms because they fall, the price of beauty being its temporary nature. The Japanese language has other words I wish English had: *kintsugi*, the art of repairing broken pottery with gold, making the damage visible and valuable; *komorebi*, sunlight filtering through leaves; *tsundoku*, the act of acquiring books and letting them pile up unread. We need more words for the specific loneliness of unread books, the promise deferred, the self we imagined we would become.

I have three hundred books I haven't read. I keep buying more. This is either hope or delusion, and I no longer know the difference.

The pigeon man died last spring. His daughter, who had never understood the birds, opened the coop and let them go. They circled the building for three days, she told me, before they finally dispersed. Miles was the last to leave. She recognized him by the white patch on his left wing, the one her father had described at the funeral, crying in a way that surprised everyone, this rough man in his sixties weeping for a pigeon named after a trumpet player dead before he was born.

I don't know what happened to Miles. Whether he found another roof, another hand. Whether he lived out whatever span pigeons live, three years, five, more if they're lucky and avoid the hawks and the poison and the children with rocks. I don't know if pigeons feel the equivalent of *aware*, if the magnetic field they follow home eventually becomes just habit, just the only thing they know to do, or if each return carries some version of relief, of rightness, of the center holding.

The morning light is different now. It's afternoon, the slant gone vertical, the dust motes invisible in the brightness. I have used most of my words and said almost nothing I planned. This is the salvage, the collapse, the something I couldn't design. The clay is still wet. The wheel still turns.

samples.result:
The morning light hit the kitchen counter at 6:47, same angle as yesterday, same dust motes performing their slow ballet through the beam. I stood there waiting for the coffee maker to finish its gurgling confession, thinking about how repetition wears grooves in the mind until what was once remarkable becomes invisible.

My grandmother kept a diary for sixty-three years. Not the reflective kind—no weather reports of the soul. Just facts. "Planted tomatoes. Rain at four. Mr. Henderson's dog in the azaleas again." I found them in a cedar chest after she died, thirty-four volumes, each day accounted for like a ledger entry in some cosmic bookkeeping. At first I felt sad for her, all that observation without interpretation. Then I noticed something. On March 14, 1987, she wrote "First robin" with an exclamation point. She never used exclamation points. That robin mattered. The restraint made it louder.

We live in an age of exclamation point inflation. Everything is amazing, devastating, unmissable. The algorithm feeds us peaks without valleys, and we wonder why we feel numb at the summit. I deleted my social media accounts in 2019, not as a statement but as an experiment. The first month felt like phantom limb syndrome, reaching for a phone that no longer held anything I wanted. By the third month, I started noticing the particular green of the maple outside my window, how it shifted from emerald to something almost black as summer deepened. I'd seen that tree for six years. Never really looked.

There's a concept in Japanese aesthetics called *wabi-sabi*: the beauty of impermanence, imperfection, incompleteness. A cracked teacup repaired with gold. A garden designed to look untended. We resist it, we Americans, with our self-improvement protocols and our pursuit of closure. We want the healed wound, not the scar. But the scar is where the interesting texture lives.

I met a woman in a used bookstore in Portland who had spent thirty years collecting rejection letters. She kept them in chronological order, three-ring binders, literary magazines and agents and publishers who passed on her novels. "The first one I cried over," she told me, running her finger down a column of names. "The fiftieth one I framed." She sold her fourth novel at sixty-one. It was about a woman who collects rejection letters. She told me the binders were her real life's work, the novels just footnotes.

We misunderstand failure. We treat it as deviation from path instead of path itself. Every successful person I've ever interviewed—and I've interviewed hundreds for magazine profiles—has a private archive of almosts and not-quites they rarely mention in the polished version. The tech founder who went bankrupt twice. The surgeon who failed her boards. The poet who didn't publish for twenty years. These aren't digressions. They're the compost everything grew from.

Memory is another liar. I remember my childhood as mostly golden, but when I found an old journal from age thirteen, I was shocked by the despair. "Everything is gray," I wrote. "I will never be happy." I don't remember that boy. He got edited out in the revision process, replaced by a nostalgic fiction that serves the present better. We're all unreliable narrators of our own lives, and that's not necessarily a flaw. The edited version might be the true one, in the way a novel is truer than a transcript.

I think about time differently as I get older. Not as sand through an hourglass—that's too passive—but as something I sculpt. Some hours I make rough and utilitarian, others I sand to smoothness. The pandemic years were strange clay. I learned to bake bread, like everyone else. I also learned that I could go three days without speaking aloud and not feel lonely. That worried me at first. Now I think it was just another way of being human, one our culture doesn't have much room for.

The last time I visited my hometown, I drove past the house where I grew up. Someone had painted it gray; it had been white. The oak tree I'd climbed was gone, probably a casualty of age or storm. I felt nothing, which felt like a betrayal of something. Shouldn't there be emotion? A swelling of soundtrack? Instead I just noted the change, like my grandmother with her tomatoes. "House is gray now. Tree removed." Maybe that's enough. Maybe the feeling comes later, in dreams, in the way certain smells still trigger something I can't name.

I've been reading about deep time. Geologists think in millions of years. The Appalachian Mountains were once as tall as the Himalayas; now they're hills, and in another hundred million years they'll be plains. Nothing we build will last. Nothing we destroy is permanent. The plastic in the oceans will eventually subduct into the mantle and be reborn as something else. This isn't comfort exactly, but it's perspective. Our urgency is real and also temporary.

I used to want to change the world. Now I want to change the room I'm in, and trust the ripple. I volunteer at a literacy center, teaching adults to read. Maria is sixty-four, came from Guatemala, works nights cleaning offices. She can read a children's book now, slowly, her finger tracing each word. The pride on her face when she finished *The Very Hungry Caterpillar*—I keep that image like a stone in my pocket, something to hold when the news gets too loud.

The news is always too loud now. We're not built for this much information, this much suffering rendered in high definition. I don't know the solution. I know that I limit my intake, that I donate to causes instead of just feeling bad, that I try to be present with the person in front of me. These are small strategies against a large problem. They don't scale. Maybe scaling isn't the point.

There's a bird that nests on the ledge outside my office window. I don't know what kind. Small, brown, unremarkable. Every spring she builds her nest in the same spot, raises her chicks, teaches them to fly. They leave. She leaves. The nest stays through winter, slowly falling apart, until she returns to build again. I watch this cycle without knowing what it means. Maybe it means persistence. Maybe it means nothing, just the bird doing what birds do. The not-knowing is its own kind of peace.

I used to need everything to mean something. Now I find meaning in the search for meaning, in the questions that stay open like doors. A friend asked me recently what I believe in. I said I believe in the conversation we're having, in the coffee growing cold, in the particular slant of light that will be different in ten minutes and gone in an hour. I believe in the temporary, which is another word for the real.

The coffee maker finished. I poured, I sat, I watched the dust motes until they disappeared into the general brightness of the day beginning. Nothing special happened. Nothing special needed to.
